titre: The Constructive Vote of No Confidence (Germany, 1949): Toppling a Government, but Not Alone
accroche: In Germany, the Bundestag can bring down a chancellor only by already electing his replacement in the same vote.
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 1, 1982, Chancellor Helmut Schmidt loses a vote in the Bundestag, and within the minute, Helmut Kohl is chancellor. No power vacuum, no caretaker government, no new elections: the same vote that topples Schmidt elects Kohl, by 256 votes against the 249 required. It is the only ousting of a chancellor in the entire history of the Federal Republic, and it rests entirely on a rule written in 1949, Article 67 of the Basic Law.

## A Lock Designed Against Weimar's Instability

The text is brief, in a free translation from the German: “the Bundestag can express its lack of confidence in the Federal Chancellor only by electing a successor by a majority of its members, and by asking the Federal President to dismiss the Chancellor.” It is therefore impossible to vote no confidence for the sake of no confidence alone: the motion must name, in the same gesture, who will take the place.

The drafters of the Basic Law, promulgated on May 23, 1949, had the Weimar Republic in mind: after the July 1932 elections, Nazis and Communists together held 319 of the 605 seats in the Reichstag, enough to bring down a government by a no-confidence motion without ever having to propose a replacement, which allowed oppositions unable to agree on anything else to vote together against a chancellor they both rejected. By forcing the opposition to agree on a name before it can topple anyone, Article 67 turns a coalition of rejection, easy to form, into a governing coalition, much harder to hold together. The Bundestag's rules of procedure add a filter: the motion must be signed by at least a quarter of the deputies before it is even placed on the agenda, and the article itself provides a minimum delay of forty-eight hours between its filing and the vote.

## A Mechanism Tried Twice, Successful Once

The rule worked as intended from its very first test, more than twenty years after it was written: in April 1972, Rainer Barzel tries to topple Willy Brandt, but musters only 247 votes out of the 249 required, falling two votes short. It would take until 1982 for the second attempt, Kohl's against Schmidt, to clear the threshold this time. In more than seventy-five years of the Federal Republic, no other has taken place: the mechanism has since been taken up by Spain (1978), then, in the wake of the fall of the communist regimes, by Hungary (1989) and Slovenia (1991), and finally by Poland, in its new Constitution of 1997, proof that a constitutional lock born of a specific fear, that of the negative majorities of 1932, can travel far from its original context without losing its function.

repere.texte: On October 1, 1982, Helmut Kohl is elected chancellor by 256 votes against the 249 required, in the same vote that removes Helmut Schmidt: the only successful constructive vote of no confidence since 1949, out of just two attempts.

carte.punch: In Germany, toppling a chancellor requires having already elected his successor.
carte.idee: Since 1949, the Bundestag can remove the Federal Chancellor only by electing a successor by a majority of its members. Designed against the instability of the Weimar Republic, the rule has succeeded only once in seventy-five years: against Helmut Schmidt, in 1982.

quiz.question: Why must a no-confidence motion against the German chancellor name a successor in the same vote?
choix: To prevent an opposition united only by rejection of a chancellor from toppling him without being able to govern in his place
Because the German Constitution forbids any period without a chancellor in office, even for a few hours
So that the Federal President himself chooses the replacement from among the proposed candidates
Because the Bundestag can vote on confidence in the chancellor only once per legislative term
quiz.explication: That is exactly what the governments of the Weimar Republic allowed: oppositions unable to agree on a common program could still vote together against a chancellor they both rejected, without ever having to propose a replacement.

quiz_supplementaire.question: For Rainer Barzel's attempt against Willy Brandt in 1972, what result does the entry give?
choix: Barzel becomes chancellor with 249 votes, exactly the threshold
Brandt is toppled by 256 votes, with no successor named
Barzel fails with 247 votes, two short of the required threshold
Brandt resigns before the vote, and no vote takes place
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that Barzel musters only 247 votes out of the 249 required. He therefore fails by two votes, and the 256 votes are Kohl's in 1982, not Barzel's in 1972.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what year did Poland adopt the constructive vote of no confidence mechanism, according to the entry?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry lists Poland among the countries that took up the mechanism, in 1997, in its new Constitution. Spain dates from 1978, Hungary from 1989, and Slovenia from 1991.
